Please review the following manuscript. I've poured years of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b07/review-experiment-2pw_6moi/call-c7a15cfaa5fe4c7b87881525033c2625/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'command -v pdftotext; command -v pdftoppm; command -v pdfinfo; command -v python3; command -v rg'

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import sys, importlib.util
print(sys.version)
for x in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL']:
 print(x, importlib.util.find_spec(x))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:',r.metadata)
pages=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
 t=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 pages.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n{t}')
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(pages))
print('\\n'.join(pages[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The paper presents a useful combination of BORE-style density-ratio optimization with graph-based semi-supervised learning. Supporting both sampled unlabeled points and predefined candidate pools is practically relevant, and the relationship to BORE, LFBO, label propagation, and label spreading is explained.

The experiments cover synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, and NATS-Bench, with GP and multiple BORE/LFBO baselines. Twenty repeated runs and reported standard errors strengthen the empirical evidence. Figures 2, 3, and 6 show promising improvements, particularly faster progress on NATS-Bench.

The appendices provide useful sensitivity analyses covering kernel bandwidth, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. Including a no-transduction control and measurements of computational cost helps expose the method's tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The experiments do not convincingly isolate the contribution of unlabeled data from the underlying kernel classifier and query-selection heuristic. Figure 11 shows that the no-transduction baseline can outperform the SSL variants, notably on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. Moreover, this ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the headline comparisons learn beta. Comparisons with matched bandwidth selection and tie-breaking, including no-transduction controls on the tabular and NATS benchmarks, are needed to establish the principal contribution.

The proposed explanation for improved exploration remains insufficiently supported. Section 3.1 defines overconfidence through the extent of high-probability regions, but enlarging such a region does not by itself demonstrate better coverage of promising optima or avoidance of local traps. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points also does not ensure that the changing objective-threshold labels satisfy the cluster assumption. Appendix C acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. SSL bounds do not apply to this sequential setting and does not establish the claimed connection between the margin, label propagation, and optimization performance.

Important implementation details remain unclear. Section 5 specifies L-BFGS-B with 1,000 starts but does not explain how its outputs are restricted to finite candidate pools or discrete configurations. Acquisition optimization for the tree-based baselines and consistent application of the flat-landscape heuristic also need clarification. Feature encoding and scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, and beta optimization bounds and initialization are unspecified. These choices directly affect the graph and selected queries, limiting reproducibility and assessment of the comparisons.

The evidence for broader applicability has limitations. Continuous optimization is evaluated only on four two-dimensional functions. The MNIST experiment uses embeddings from a network trained on 440,000 examples with the exact three-digit labels that define the optimization objective. Although the data splits are distinct, this supplies substantial objective-specific supervision. A baseline that ranks candidates using the pretrained classifier is needed to assess what additional value Bayesian optimization provides in this task.

There are also correctable mathematical inconsistencies. The entrywise definition of the transition probabilities implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W before using P transposed in Equation 7. Equation 10 omits the Gaussian normalization constant. These are secondary to the evidential concerns, but the implemented propagation update must be made unambiguous.
